d: What a crawler is for, the three-step loop, scoping questions, the four traits of a good crawler, and the napkin math
winTitle: Scoped, sized and ready to crawl!
goal: Your win today: you can explain what a crawler does in one breath, ask the five scoping questions, name the four traits (scalable, robust, polite, extensible), and work out ~400 pages/s, ~800 peak, 500 TB a month and 30 PB over five years.
bookSections: Chapter intro (what crawlers are used for); Step 1: Understand the problem and establish design scope (basic algorithm, scoping dialogue, characteristics of a good crawler, back-of-the-envelope estimation)

stages.title: Why send a spider?
stages.teaches: A web crawler (also called a robot or spider) is a program that discovers new and updated content on the web: pages, images, videos, PDFs. It starts from a small set of pages and follows the links on them to find more. The book lists four uses: (1) search engine indexing, the most common, e.g. Googlebot building Google's index; (2) web archiving, saving pages for the future, e.g. national libraries such as the US Library of Congress and the EU web archive; (3) web mining, pulling knowledge out of the web, e.g. finance firms downloading shareholder-meeting transcripts and annual reports; (4) web monitoring, watching for copyright and trademark infringement, e.g. Digimarc hunting pirated works. How hard a crawler is depends on scale: a class project can be done in an afternoon; a crawler for the whole web needs a dedicated team.
stages.interaction: Sort-into-bins: four labelled baskets (Indexing, Archiving, Mining, Monitoring) and 8 cards that drop in one at a time, e.g. 'A search engine refreshes what it knows about new blog posts' → Indexing; 'A national library keeps a copy of government sites before an election' → Archiving; 'A hedge fund collects every company's annual report' → Mining; 'A record label searches for leaked albums' → Monitoring; 'A price-comparison site gathers product prices daily' → Mining; 'A brand checks for fake shops using its logo' → Monitoring; 'Crawl the web so search results include yesterday's news' → Indexing; 'Preserve a defunct game studio's website' → Archiving. Drag (or tap card then tap basket). Wrong drops bounce back with a one-line hint. A small spider mascot crawls one step across a web graphic per correct card.
stages.check: All 8 cards placed correctly (retries allowed). Then Q.quiz, 1 question: 'Which use does this chapter design for?' → search engine indexing.

stages.title: The three-step loop
stages.teaches: The basic algorithm is a loop: (1) given a set of URLs, download every page they point to; (2) extract the URLs found in those pages; (3) add the new URLs to the list still to be downloaded, then go back to step 1. The starting URLs are called seeds. The web is a graph: pages are nodes, links are edges, so crawling is graph traversal. The simple loop hides the hard parts this world covers: duplicates, politeness, priority, scale, broken servers and traps.
stages.interaction: Step-through simulation. On screen: a mini web of 12 page nodes (a small fixed graph with a cycle, e.g. A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→A, …), a 'To download' list on the left seeded with A, and a 'Downloaded' list on the right. Buttons: 'Download', 'Extract links', 'Add to list'. Each press animates that step: the page lights up, its outgoing link arrows glow, and the found URLs fly into the To-download list. Before round 2 the learner predicts: 'After downloading B and C, how many times will D appear in the list if we add every link we find?' (choices 0 / 1 / 2); answer 2, and D→A also re-adds A. The sim then shows the list filling with repeats and a counter 'wasted downloads'. Banner at the end: 'The naive loop re-downloads pages and loops forever on cycles. Quest 9.2 adds the fix.'
stages.check: Prediction made (wrong prediction costs no heart, shows the reason) and graph fully explored. Q.quiz with 2 questions: order the three steps; 'What is a seed URL?' → the starting set the crawl begins from.

stages.title: Ask before you crawl
stages.teaches: Scoping answers from the book's interview dialogue: purpose is search engine indexing; about 1 billion pages are collected per month; content is HTML only; newly added and edited pages must be picked up; crawled HTML is stored for up to 5 years; pages with duplicate content are ignored. Lesson: even a 'simple' prompt hides choices that change the design, so pin down purpose, scale, content types, freshness, retention and duplicates before drawing.
stages.interaction: Question deck like 8.1: 10 cards, learner taps the 6 good ones. Good: 'What is the crawler for?', 'How many pages per month?', 'Which content types: HTML only, or images and PDFs too?', 'Do we need to pick up new and edited pages?', 'Do we store the pages, and for how long?', 'What about duplicate content?'. Distractors: 'Python or Go?', 'Should I use Elasticsearch?', 'What's the logo?', 'Can we skip robots.txt to go faster?' (shake + note: 'politeness is a requirement, not a knob you negotiate away'). Each good card flips to show the interviewer's answer and pins it to a 'Requirements' sticky note that stays visible for the rest of the quest.
stages.check: All 6 good cards flipped. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'What happens to a page whose content we've already stored under another URL?' → ignored; 'How long do we keep HTML?' → up to 5 years.

stages.title: Four traits of a good spider
stages.teaches: Beyond the functional asks, the book names four qualities. Scalability: the web has billions of pages, so crawling must run in parallel. Robustness: the web is full of traps: bad HTML, servers that never answer, crashes, malicious links; the crawler must cope without falling over. Politeness: don't fire too many requests at one website in a short time. Extensibility: adding a new content type (say, images) should need minimal change, not a rewrite.
stages.interaction: Match-the-headline: 8 short 'incident report' cards, each tapped onto one of four trait shields. 'A site's HTML has 3,000 unclosed tags and the parser crashes the whole worker' → Robust; 'A small bakery's site goes down because we hit it 50 times a second' → Polite; 'Product wants PDFs crawled next quarter and we'd have to rewrite the downloader' → Extensible; 'One machine can only fetch 50 pages a second, we need 400' → Scalable; 'A link generates infinite calendar pages' → Robust; 'A host emails us complaining about our bot' → Polite; 'We add a new server and must redistribute work' → Scalable; 'Legal wants a copyright-monitor module' → Extensible. Each shield glows when it has two correct cards.
stages.check: All 8 matched. Q.quiz 1 question: 'Which trait is about the websites, not about us?' → Politeness.

stages.title: Napkin math
stages.teaches: Assume 1 billion pages per month. QPS: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 30 days ÷ 24 h ÷ 3,600 s ≈ 386, round to about 400 pages per second. Peak QPS is taken as 2 × average = 800. Average page size is assumed to be 500 KB, so 1 billion × 500 KB = 500 TB of new storage per month. Keeping it 5 years: 500 TB × 12 × 5 = 30 PB. Tip: a month is about 2.6 million seconds; say your assumptions out loud and round.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check: four input boxes (average pages/s, peak pages/s, storage per month, storage for 5 years) with unit dropdowns (K/M/B and GB/TB/PB). Accept within ±10% (avg 350–440, peak 700–880, monthly 450–550 TB, total 27–33 PB). A 'hint' button per box reveals the formula. When all four are correct, they turn into live outputs driven by sliders: pages/month (100M–10B), peak multiplier (1×–5×), average page size (50 KB–2 MB), years kept (1–10). Mini-challenge: 'A real HTML page is often closer to 100 KB than 500 KB. Drag the size slider to 100 KB. What happens to the 5-year total?' (→ 6 PB). A side note card: 'Pages per server: if one server fetches ~50 pages/s, how many servers for peak?' (800 ÷ 50 = 16, before redundancy).
stages.check: All four boxes correct; then Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'If the target became 10 billion pages a month, average QPS ≈ ?' (≈ 4,000); 'Which assumption dominates the storage total?' → average page size × page count (and retention years).

stages.title: Boss: The Scope Sphinx
stages.sub: Which trait or number does each ask hit?
stages.teaches: Applying the four traits and the estimates to fresh requests.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'scale', label:'Scalability', sub:'more parallel work'}, {k:'robust', label:'Robustness', sub:'survive the bad web'}, {k:'polite', label:'Politeness', sub:'be kind to hosts'}, {k:'ext', label:'Extensibility', sub:'plug in new stuff'}]. Scenarios (7): 'The interviewer doubles the target to 2 billion pages a month' → scale; 'A site responds with a 30-second stall on every request' → robust; 'A university IT team says our bot looks like a DoS attack' → polite; 'We now need to crawl images for an image search' → ext; 'One downloader machine dies mid-crawl' → robust; 'Every link on Wikipedia points back to Wikipedia, and we'd fetch it in a burst' → polite; 'Peak traffic is 2× average and we sized for the average' → scale. Each 'why' ties back to the definition.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The first five minutes of the interview, compact.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'The interviewer says: design a web crawler. Give me your scoping and estimates.' Placeholder: 'First I'd ask what it's for…'. Model: 'I'd confirm the purpose, say search indexing, and the scale: a billion pages a month, HTML only, we pick up new and changed pages, keep the HTML for five years, and skip duplicate content. The loop is download, extract links, add new links, repeat, starting from seed URLs. I'd want it scalable, robust to bad pages and dead servers, polite to the sites we hit, and extensible to new content types. A billion a month is about 400 pages a second, call it 800 at peak. At 500 KB a page that's 500 TB a month and 30 PB over five years.' Checks: ['I asked about purpose, scale, content type, freshness, retention and duplicates', 'I named the four traits', 'I said ~400/s average and ~800/s peak', 'I said 500 TB a month and 30 PB over 5 years'].

caveats: 1 billion ÷ 2.59 million seconds is really about 386 pages/s; the book rounds to 400. Rounding up is fine and interviewers expect it.
'Peak = 2× average' is a rule of thumb, not a law. A crawler controls its own pace, so unlike a user-facing service its peak is mostly a choice; the bigger risk is uneven load per host.
500 KB per page is generous for HTML alone (HTML documents are often tens of KB, and they compress well). The 30 PB figure is an upper bound before compression and de-duplication.
Real search crawls are much larger than 1 billion pages a month, and Common Crawl alone publishes billions of pages per crawl. The number is an interview-sized target, not Google's.
